title: Describing the need: SOW, PWS and SOO
summary: Before you can buy anything, the customer has to describe what they need. Describe it by the results you want, not by a brand or a step-by-step method, so the most companies can compete. For services, that usually means a performance work statement and a plan to check the work.
why: A bad requirement causes most of the trouble that follows: protests, disputes, cost overruns and unhappy customers. The exam tests requirement types and performance-based acquisition under Plan Solicitation.

sections.h: Three ways to describe a requirement
sections.body:
- **Statement of work (SOW):** says what to do and often how. Common for supplies with specifications and for design-heavy work.
- **Performance work statement (PWS):** says what results are required and how they will be measured, and leaves the how to the contractor. It is the heart of performance-based acquisition (FAR 37.1).
- **Statement of objectives (SOO):** a short statement of the Government's goals. Offerors propose their own PWS in response.

State needs in terms of functions to be performed, performance required, or essential physical characteristics, so as many sources as possible can compete (FAR 11.102). Use existing standards rather than inventing new ones.

Naming a brand, or features only one manufacturer has, limits competition. That needs a justification: for actions above the simplified acquisition threshold, a brand-name requirement is a sole-source justification under FAR 6.103-1(d) (see FAR 11.204).

- **Personal services:** contracts that make contractor employees work like Government employees, under continuous Government supervision, are prohibited unless a law allows them (FAR 37.201-2).
- **Inherently governmental functions:** decisions only Government employees may make, such as awarding contracts, approving requirements or directing other employees, cannot be contracted out (FAR 7.503, 37.3).

example.title: Grass, not mowers
example.body: A customer's first draft says: 'Contractor shall mow every Tuesday with a 60-inch riding mower.' A performance version says: 'Keep grass between 2 and 4 inches; inspections monthly; 95% of areas must meet the standard.' The second lets companies use their own equipment and schedules, often at a lower price, and tells the COR exactly what to check.

remember: SOW = how; PWS = results and measures; SOO = goals only.
Results, standards, surveillance: the three parts of performance-based.
mistakes: Copying last year's SOW without asking whether the need changed.
Writing a PWS that directs contractor staff hour by hour: that drifts into personal services.

title: Market research
summary: Market research means finding out who can meet the need, what it costs, and how the market sells it, before you decide how to buy. It drives almost every later decision: commercial or not, set-aside or not, contract type and price.
why: Market research is required by law in many situations and supports competition, small business and pricing decisions. It is part of the 12 Plan Solicitation questions.

sections.body: Do market research appropriate to the circumstances before you develop new requirements documents, and before you solicit or place an order above the simplified acquisition threshold. Document the results in proportion to the size and complexity of the buy (FAR 10.001). The rules put commercial products and services first: look for them before anything custom.

- Search prior buys and existing contracts for the same thing.
- Search SAM.gov for registered businesses and similar opportunities.
- Check GSA Advantage and other catalogs for commercial prices.
- Post a **sources sought** notice or **request for information (RFI)** (FAR 5.103 special notices).
- Hold an **industry day** or one-on-one meetings; early exchanges with industry are encouraged, as long as everyone gets the same information (FAR 15.101).
- Talk to the customer, other contracting offices and the small business professional.

- Are there commercial items or services that meet the need?
- How many capable sources exist? Are at least two of them small businesses?
- What are typical prices, terms, warranties and delivery times?
- How does industry usually sell this (fixed price, hourly, subscription)?
- Are there required sources or existing contracts you must check?
Write a market research report or memo: what you searched, whom you contacted, what you found and what you concluded. The DPC Market Research Guide (on the DPCAP website) offers templates.

example.title: Is there a small business that can do this?
example.body: Your customer wants a five-year maintenance contract for HVAC systems. A sources sought notice draws responses from four small businesses with relevant experience and prices that look reasonable. That supports a small business set-aside. Without the notice, you would have had nothing to base that decision on.

remember: Before the requirement, and before soliciting above the SAT: research.
Commercial first: look for what the market already sells.
mistakes: Sharing the incumbent's prices or the IGCE in a sources sought notice.
Treating market research as a form to fill out after the decisions are made.

title: Required sources and existing contracts
summary: Before you buy on the open market, check whether the law requires you to use a particular source, and whether an existing contract can already meet the need. FAR Part 8 sets the order.
why: Skipping a required source is a classic error. FAR Part 8 is one of the 20 part titles on the exam (Required Sources of Supplies and Services).

sections.body:
FAR Part 8 lists sources you must use for certain supplies and services:
- Agency inventories and excess property, when they fit the need.
- **AbilityOne:** products and services on the AbilityOne Procurement List, made or performed by nonprofit agencies employing people who are blind or have significant disabilities (FAR 8.2).
- **Federal Prison Industries (FPI, also called UNICOR):** for supplies it makes, after market research shows its product is comparable in price, quality and delivery (FAR 8.3).
- Government printing rules for printing.

Look for contracts that already cover the need: your agency's or another agency's indefinite-delivery contracts, governmentwide contracts and the GSA Federal Supply Schedules (FAR 8.104, 8.4). Ordering from them is often faster and still competitive. Schedule ordering procedures are now in GSA's own regulation (GSAR 538.71).
Using another agency's contract or contracting office has its own rules, including a written agreement and, for some vehicles, a business-case analysis (FAR 17.5).

example.title: Office furniture
example.body: Your customer wants new chairs. Before asking local vendors for quotes, you check whether the chairs are on the AbilityOne list or made by FPI, and whether your office already has a furniture BPA. Each check takes minutes and keeps the buy legal.

remember: Check required sources, then existing contracts, then the open market.
AbilityOne and FPI are the names to know.
mistakes: Starting with open-market quotes before checking AbilityOne and FPI.
Assuming a GSA order needs no competition or documentation. Ordering rules still apply.

title: Small business programs
summary: The Government must give small businesses a fair share of its contracts. Above the micro-purchase threshold, if you reasonably expect offers from at least two responsible small businesses at fair market prices, you must set the buy aside for small business: the rule of two.
why: Small business decisions come early in almost every buy and FAR Part 19 (Small Business) is on the exam's list of part titles.

sections.body: The Small Business Administration (SBA) sets size standards by industry, using NAICS codes. The contracting officer picks the NAICS code that best describes the work, and that code's size standard decides who counts as small (FAR 19.103).

For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, the contracting officer must set the contract aside for small business when there is a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses that are competitive on fair market price, quality and delivery. If you do not set it aside, document why (FAR 19.104-1). The rule does not apply at or below the micro-purchase threshold or to required sources under Part 8.

- **8(a) Business Development:** firms owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people; awards can be competitive among 8(a) firms or, under limits, sole source through SBA (FAR 19.108).
- **HUBZone:** firms in historically underutilized business zones (FAR 19.105).
- **Service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB)** (FAR 19.106).
- **Women-owned small business (WOSB)** and economically disadvantaged WOSB (FAR 19.107).

Set-asides for these programs are allowed; the contracting officer considers them using market research.

Coordinate with your agency's small business professional and, where required, the SBA procurement center representative (FAR 19.102). Large contracts with subcontracting opportunities need a small business subcontracting plan from large-business awardees (FAR 19.109).

FAR Part 19 applies in the United States and its outlying areas; outside them, agencies may apply it but are not required to (FAR 19.000(b)). Many 51Cs work overseas, so ask your office how it handles set-asides abroad.

example.title: The janitorial contract
example.body: Market research for a $600,000-a-year custodial contract finds six small businesses with relevant experience and competitive prices. The rule of two is met, so the contract is set aside for small business. If only one small business had responded, you would document why it was not set aside and compete it full and open.

remember: Two responsible small businesses + fair market prices = set it aside.
NAICS code picks the size standard.
mistakes: Choosing a NAICS code that fits the buyer's plan instead of the work.
Skipping the small business professional's review.

title: Competition and sole-source justifications
summary: By law, the Government must use full and open competition unless a specific exception applies. When you cannot compete, you need the right legal authority and a written justification, approved at the level the dollar value requires.
why: FAR Part 6 (Competition Requirements) is on the exam's part-title list, and competition decisions are protest magnets.

sections.body:
- **Full and open:** every responsible source may compete (FAR 6.101).
- **Full and open after excluding sources:** for example, a small business set-aside, which is still full and open competition among the eligible firms (FAR 6.102).
- **Other than full and open:** only when one of the seven statutory exceptions applies (FAR 6.103).

At or below the simplified acquisition threshold, you still promote competition. For commercial buys, document why only one source is available (FAR 12.102(a)); for noncommercial buys, soliciting a single source needs a determination and findings (FAR 13.101(b)).

example.title: Only one company makes the part
example.body: A radar system needs a replacement circuit card that only the original manufacturer can supply because it owns the design data. That fits 6.103-1. You write the justification with your market research, the reason no one else can do it, and what the office will do to allow competition in the future, then route it for approval at the level its value requires.

remember: Full and open is the rule; seven exceptions; justify in writing; approve by dollar level.
A set-aside is not an exception to competition.
mistakes: Calling a set-aside 'sole source'.
Citing the old 6.302 numbers or the FAR approval table instead of DoW's Table 206-1.

title: Acquisition planning and the IGCE
summary: Acquisition planning pulls everyone together to decide how a requirement will be bought before any solicitation goes out. The independent Government cost estimate (IGCE) is the Government's own estimate of what the work should cost.
why: Plan Solicitation is 12 exam questions, and FAR Part 7 (Acquisition Planning) is on the part-title list. Late or thin planning is the main reason buys miss their dates.

sections.body:
- **Make or buy:** do it in-house or buy it.
- **Supplies or services:** different rules, clauses and funding.
- **Delivery schedule:** realistic dates the market can meet.
- **Government-furnished property or information:** what the Government provides the contractor.
- **Consolidation and bundling:** combining requirements can shut out small businesses, so it needs market research and a written determination (FAR 7.107-2).

The requiring activity prepares the IGCE, independent of any contractor's numbers. You use it to check that funds are enough, to judge whether offered prices are reasonable, and to plan negotiations. Protect it: the IGCE is not shared with offerors.

Planning includes time for every step: market research, documents, reviews, posting, evaluation and award. Your office likely publishes standard lead times by type of action. Customers who know them submit on time.

example.title: The September surprise
example.body: In August a customer submits a $4 million services requirement that must start 1 October. The office's lead time for that kind of buy is 120 days. Early planning would have caught this in the spring. Now the team has to look at options like extending the current contract, which needs its own justification, instead of a clean competition.

remember: Plan early, as a team, for the whole life of the buy.
The IGCE belongs to the Government: never share it with offerors.
mistakes: Letting a contractor write the IGCE.
Planning the award but not the administration and closeout.

title: Contract types
summary: The contract type decides who carries the cost risk. In a fixed-price contract the contractor carries it; in a cost-reimbursement contract the Government does. Choose the type that fits how well the work and its cost can be defined.
why: FAR Part 16 (Types of Contracts) is on the exam list, and contract type comes up in planning, pricing and administration questions.

sections.body:
- **Firm-fixed-price (FFP):** one price, no matter what it costs the contractor. Most risk on the contractor, least administration. Preferred when requirements and prices are clear (FAR 16.202).
- **Fixed-price with economic price adjustment (FP-EPA):** FFP plus adjustments for specific market changes, such as fuel or steel prices.
- **Fixed-price incentive (FPIF):** a target cost, target profit and ceiling price, with a share ratio that rewards the contractor for coming in under target.

For commercial products and services, use FFP or FP-EPA (FAR 12.104).

The Government pays allowable costs up to a ceiling, plus a fee. Use it only when costs cannot be estimated well enough for a fixed price, the contractor has an adequate accounting system, and the Government can watch costs (FAR 16.301).
- **Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF):** the fee is set at award.
- **Cost-plus-incentive-fee (CPIF):** the fee moves with cost results.
- **Cost-plus-award-fee (CPAF):** the fee is earned through subjective evaluation of performance.
- **Cost** and **cost-sharing:** no fee (for nonprofits, or when the contractor benefits).

Payment by hourly rates (which include profit) plus materials at cost. The contractor has little reason to control hours, so these are the least preferred and need a determination that no other type is suitable, a ceiling price and close surveillance (FAR 16.601).

- **Indefinite-delivery indefinite-quantity (IDIQ):** a minimum and maximum quantity; you place orders as needs arise. Multiple-award IDIQs require fair opportunity among awardees when ordering (FAR 16.504, 16.507).
- **Requirements:** the Government buys all its actual needs of an item from one contractor for a period.
- **Definite quantity:** a fixed quantity delivered over time.
- **Letter contract:** a quick start when work must begin at once, definitized later; tightly limited.
Pick the type that best spreads risk given how well the work and cost can be predicted, then write down why (FAR 16.101, 16.103). As a requirement matures, move toward fixed price.

example.title: From research to production
example.body: A new sensor's first prototype cannot be priced reliably: cost-plus-fixed-fee makes sense. Two years later, with a stable design and real cost history, the production buy can move to firm-fixed-price. The contract type follows the uncertainty.

remember: Fixed price: contractor carries cost risk. Cost type: Government carries it.
T&M is the last resort: no incentive to control hours.
mistakes: Using cost-reimbursement for well-defined commercial work.
Using T&M without a ceiling price and a D&F.

title: Choosing the method: micro-purchase to negotiation
summary: The dollar value and the kind of item decide how you buy. Small buys can use a purchase card. Up to the simplified acquisition threshold, simplified procedures apply. Larger buys use sealed bidding or negotiation. Since the FAR Overhaul, commercial simplified buys follow Part 12, and Part 13 covers only noncommercial ones.
why: Knowing which procedure and threshold apply is basic to every buy, and FAR Parts 12, 13 and 15 are all on the exam's part-title list.

sections.body:
- **Micro-purchase threshold:** $15,000 (higher for contingency and emergency buys: $25,000 inside the U.S., $40,000 outside).
- **Simplified acquisition threshold (SAT):** $350,000 ($1 million inside the U.S. and $2 million outside for contingency and emergency buys).
- **Simplified procedures for commercial products and services:** up to $9 million ($15 million for contingency and emergency).

These come from FAR 2.101 and were raised for inflation on 1 October 2025. Check FAR & key numbers for the current figures.

At or below the micro-purchase threshold, purchases can be made without competitive quotes if the price is reasonable, usually with the Government purchase card (GPC) by trained cardholders. Spread purchases among qualified suppliers when practical (FAR 12.4; 13.401 points there). Splitting a requirement to stay under a threshold is prohibited.

- **Commercial (FAR 12.201-1):** a request for quotations followed by a purchase order, up to $9 million. At or below the SAT, solicit quotes from at least three sources when practicable. Evaluation is flexible: no formal evaluation plan or competitive range is required (12.203).
- **Noncommercial (FAR Part 13):** only when no commercial product or service meets the need, up to the SAT. Do not split requirements to fit under the SAT (13.001).
- Either way, the contracting officer determines the price is fair and reasonable and documents the procedures used (12.204, 13.203). BPAs can make repeat buys easy; each call under a BPA must stay at or below the SAT (13.201).

- **Sealed bidding (Part 14):** invitation for bids, public bid opening, award to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder, no discussions. Use it when price is the deciding factor and specifications are clear.
- **Contracting by negotiation (Part 15):** request for proposals, evaluation on price and non-price factors, discussions allowed. Use it for larger or complex buys where you need to weigh more than price.

example.title: Three buys, three methods
example.body:
- $4,200 of toner: a cardholder buys it with the GPC.
- $180,000 of commercial furniture: an RFQ under FAR 12.201-1 to at least three sources, a purchase order to the best value.
- $6 million custom training simulator: a Part 15 request for proposals with technical and price evaluation.

remember: MPT $15K, SAT $350K, commercial simplified $9M.
Commercial simplified = Part 12; noncommercial simplified = Part 13.
mistakes: Splitting one requirement into several small buys to avoid a threshold.
Using Part 13 procedures for a commercial buy after the FAR Overhaul.

title: Buying commercial products and services
summary: If the market already sells it to the public, buy it the commercial way: use commercial terms, keep Government-unique requirements to a minimum, and use the streamlined commercial clauses and procedures in FAR Part 12.
why: Most of what a new specialist buys is commercial. FAR Part 12 is on the exam list, and the FAR Overhaul moved commercial simplified buying into it.

sections.body: FAR 2.101 defines commercial products and commercial services. In short: items or services of a type customarily used by the general public or nongovernmental entities and sold, leased or offered to them, plus some minor modifications and related services. Market research tells you whether a need can be met commercially.

Agencies must prefer commercial products and services, and commercial components when buying noncommercial items (FAR 12.101). You may not restrict competition to one commercial brand or source without the justification Part 6 requires (FAR 12.102).

- **Contract type:** firm-fixed-price or fixed-price with economic price adjustment (12.104).
- **Solicitation:** you may use a combined synopsis and solicitation, one notice that serves as both (12.202(b)).
- **Clauses:** the 52.212 family: instructions to offerors (52.212-1), evaluation (52.212-2), the terms and conditions (52.212-4), and the clause listing the statutes that apply (52.212-5) (12.205).
- **Procedures:** up to $9 million you may use the simplified procedures of 12.201-1; above that, 12.201-2 points to other procedures, often Part 15.
- **Terminations:** handled under the commercial clause, not FAR Part 49 (12.304).

Commercial terms make the Government an easier customer, bring in more companies (including non-traditional ones), and usually mean lower prices and faster delivery. Certified cost or pricing data are not required for commercial items (FAR 15.403-2).

example.title: Commercial laptops
example.body: The unit needs 200 laptops. They are sold to the public, so this is a commercial buy. You use a combined synopsis and solicitation with 52.212-1, -2, -4 and -5, a firm-fixed price, and evaluate quotes under 12.201-1. No certified cost or pricing data are needed.

remember: Commercial = Part 12 + 52.212 clauses + fixed price.
One notice can be both synopsis and solicitation.
mistakes: Adding Government-unique clauses a commercial seller will not accept.
Requesting certified cost or pricing data for a commercial item.

title: Publicizing and the solicitation
summary: Tell industry what you plan to buy, give them enough time to respond, and send a solicitation that clearly says what you want, how to respond and how you will choose. Treat every potential offeror the same.
why: Request Offers is 12 exam questions, and FAR Part 5 (Publicizing Contract Actions) is on the part-title list.

sections.body:
- A **presolicitation notice** is required for actions expected to exceed $20,000, unless an exemption applies (5.101). For $20,000 to $25,000 it stays posted 10 days; above $25,000 it goes up at least 15 days before the solicitation is issued. For commercial buys above the SAT, the notice can be combined with the solicitation.
- Notices go on the Governmentwide point of entry: **SAM.gov**.
- Exemptions include buys at or below the SAT when the solicitation itself is posted for electronic response, national security, orders under existing contracts and some other cases (5.101(b)).

- At or below the SAT and for commercial buys (not covered by trade agreements): a reasonable time to respond.
- Most other noncommercial buys: at least 30 days after the solicitation is issued.
- Research and development: 45 days from the notice.
- Buys covered by trade agreements have their own minimums.
(FAR 5, Table 5-3.)

- **Request for quotations (RFQ):** simplified buys; quotes are not offers.
- **Invitation for bids (IFB):** sealed bidding; award on price to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder.
- **Request for proposals (RFP):** negotiated buys; proposals are offers.

Larger solicitations use the uniform contract format (FAR 15.109): the schedule (what is being bought, prices, delivery, inspection and administration), the clauses, documents and attachments, and the representations and instructions. Two sections matter most to offerors:
- **Instructions:** what to submit and how (often called Section L).
- **Evaluation:** the factors and how they will be weighed (often called Section M).
The two must line up: ask for what you will evaluate, and evaluate what you asked for.

- Answer questions in writing and share the answers with everyone.
- Change the solicitation with a written **amendment** when requirements, terms or dates change, and give offerors time to respond.
- Pre-proposal conferences and site visits are fine if every offeror gets the same information.

example.title: The quiet question
example.body: One vendor calls and asks whether the Government would accept a different delivery schedule. If the answer could change what others propose, you put the question and answer, without the vendor's name, in an amendment for everyone. Answering only the caller gives that firm an unfair edge and invites a protest.

remember: Notice above $20K; 15 days ahead above $25K; 30 days to respond for most noncommercial buys.
Section L asks; Section M evaluates; they must match.
mistakes: Answering one offeror's question privately.
Evaluating a factor the solicitation never mentioned.

title: The seller's side of the deal
summary: Six exam questions look at contracting from the company's side: how a business decides whether to bid, builds its plan and price, teams with others and submits an offer. Understanding it makes you a better buyer.
why: Plan Sales and Prepare Offer are seller job tasks in the competency model (3 questions each). Knowing how industry thinks helps you write solicitations companies can answer well.

sections.body: Companies track upcoming opportunities on SAM.gov and agency forecasts, meet customers at industry days, and size up competitors. When a solicitation comes out, they read it closely, ask for clarification of anything unclear, and may propose changes. Then they decide: **bid or no-bid**, based on fit, the chance of winning, risk and profit.

- Read every requirement and make sure the company can meet all of them.
- Plan how to do the work (the technical approach) and who will do it.
- Build a **pricing strategy**: costs, risk, the competition and how the Government will evaluate price.
- Write terms that manage risk, within what the solicitation allows.
- Decide on **teaming**: a prime contractor with subcontractors, or a joint venture. Teams usually sign nondisclosure and teaming agreements.
- Submit on time, in the format required, and confirm the Government received it. Late offers are generally not considered.

- Clear, stable requirements and realistic schedules get more and better offers.
- Unclear evaluation criteria lead to protests.
- Excessive risk shifted onto contractors drives up prices or drives companies away.
- A fair process keeps good companies coming back.

example.title: The no-bid
example.body: A strong small business decides not to bid on your solicitation because the PWS hides a large, unpriced surge requirement and gives only 10 days to respond. Two other firms do bid, at high prices that cover the unknown risk. A clear surge clause and 30 days might have brought in more competition and better prices.

remember: Bid or no-bid is a business decision about fit, odds, risk and profit.
Your solicitation shapes every offer you get.
mistakes: Assuming a low number of offers means the market is small, rather than that the solicitation was hard to answer.
Forgetting that teaming and subcontracting are normal and legal.
